title: The One Thing You Can Still See
subtitle: On the wilderness, the weight, and where the eyes go
teaser: A promise about renewed strength that was spoken to people who were already spent, a Greek word used once and never found again, and a prophet who asked to die and was handed breakfast. Endurance turns out to be a question of attention, and rest turns out to come first.
theme: The strength for the race is renewed in the waiting, and the waiting is governed by what the eyes are fixed on.
framework: Hebrews 12:1-2 — let us run with patience the race that is set before us, Looking unto Jesus

modules.passage: Hast thou not known? hast thou not heard, that the everlasting God, the Lord, the Creator of the ends of the earth, fainteth not, neither is weary? there is no searching of his understanding. He giveth power to the faint; and to them that have no might he increaseth strength. Even the youths shall faint and be weary, and the young men shall utterly fall: But they that wait upon the Lord shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint.
emphasis: they that wait upon the Lord shall renew their strength
they shall run, and not be weary
modules.scriptureContext: Two minutes with a promise that was not made to people who still had energy left.

modules.definition: to wait, to look for, to hope, to expect — a waiting that leans forward
modules.usage: This is the word under "they that wait upon the Lord," and it is not the word for killing time. Brown-Driver-Briggs connects it to a root meaning to bind together, perhaps by twisting — the way loose strands become a cord — though the lexicon prints that derivation with a "perhaps" attached, and it is worth holding as loosely as the lexicon does. What is not in doubt is the posture. It shows up about forty-nine times in the Old Testament, and in almost every one of them somebody is leaning toward something they cannot yet see.

modules.heading: Who This Was Said To
modules.content:
Isaiah 40 opens the long second movement of the book, and it opens with the word comfort, said twice. Speak tenderly to Jerusalem. Her forced labour has been completed. That is the room this promise is spoken into — not a training camp, but the far end of an exile, addressed to people who have already been spent.

Which is why the verse just before it says what it says. Even youths shall faint and be weary, and the young men shall utterly fall. The passage rules out the reading a tired person is most likely to reach for, that renewal is what happens to people who had reserves to begin with. Youth is precisely what the verse disqualifies.

Then notice the order of what is promised. Mount up with wings as eagles. Run, and not be weary. Walk, and not faint. It descends. The spectacular thing comes first and the ordinary thing comes last, which is backwards from how anyone would build the sentence for effect — unless walking is the harder of the three, and the one most of a life is actually made of.

And all three of them sit downstream of one verb. They that wait. Not they that try again, or they that press through, or they that find it in themselves. The strength in this passage is renewed, which is a word for something being given back, and the condition attached to it is the one thing an exhausted person is usually least willing to do.

modules.prompt: Where are you being asked to keep going on strength you no longer have? Name the place plainly, without deciding yet what to do about it.

modules.heading: A Two-Minute Prayer
modules.prayerText: Lord, You do not grow tired. We do. We have been running on what was left and calling it faithfulness. Teach us to wait on You before we ask You to bless our exhaustion. Amen.

modules.ctaSubtext: That can be the whole of today. Below, when there is time: three Greek words that turn out to describe the same problem from three sides, a prophet who was handed bread and sleep before he was handed a word, and a blind poet arguing himself out of a complaint in fourteen lines.

modules.passage: Wherefore seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us, and let us run with patience the race that is set before us, Looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith; who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is set down at the right hand of the throne of God.
modules.transliteration: aphorōntes — "looking away from everything else, at"
emphasis: the joy that was set before him
modules.scriptureContext: The instruction and its mechanism in a single sentence: run with patience, by looking at one thing.

modules.heading: The Weight, and the Thing That Stands All Around
modules.content:
There are two problems in the first half of that sentence and they are not the same problem. Lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us.

The first is ὄγκος (ogkos). It means bulk, mass, a thing with heft. It carries no moral charge whatsoever. A runner sheds it not because it is wicked but because it is heavy, and the passage is careful enough to name it separately from the sin sitting next to it in the same clause. Some of what has to come off a life is not sin. It is just weight.

The second is εὐπερίστατος (euperistatos), and it is a strange word to run into. It appears once in the New Testament and, as far as anyone has found, nowhere else in surviving Greek. Thayer builds a meaning out of its parts — skilfully surrounding, besetting, namely, to prevent or retard running — and then notes, in the same entry, that the word is not found anywhere else. Strong's renders the same picture as a competitor thwarting a racer in every direction. Whatever else it means, the shape of it is spatial. Something standing all the way around.

Then comes the word for how to run: ὑπομονή (hypomonē). The King James prints it patience. Almost every modern translation prints it endurance. They are the same Greek word, and English needing two words for it is the difficulty in miniature — patience sounds like something done sitting still, endurance sounds like something done at effort, and the Greek has no interest in the distinction. In the writer's mind they are not two things.

One more detail, easy to skim past. The cloud of witnesses is not a stadium of finishers. Hebrews 11 has just introduced every one of them, and the chapter's own summary is blunt: they all died in faith, without having received the things they were promised. So the crowd surrounding the reader is not made of people waving from the far side of the finish line. It is made of people who ran the entire distance without ever seeing the end of it. For anyone in a long season with no visible edge to it, that is a different kind of company, and a more useful one.

modules.definition: to look away from all else at one object; to fix the eyes upon
modules.usage: It occurs twice in the whole New Testament. Once in Philippians 2:23, where Paul says he will send Timothy as soon as he sees how things turn out for himself, and once here. The form in Hebrews 12:2 is ἀφορῶντες (aphorōntes), a present participle — which in Greek carries continuing action rather than a single completed act. Not a glance taken at the starting line. A keeping-on-looking, for the length of the race.
modules.usageNote: The prefix is doing half the work, and most English renderings lose it. ἀπό (apo) means away from; ὁράω (horaō) means to see. Abbott-Smith keeps both halves in his gloss — looking away from all else, to fix one's gaze upon — and Thayer's is the same shape: to turn the eyes away from other things and fix them on something. So the instruction is not simply to concentrate harder. It is a turning away that is also a turning toward, and the two are one motion. You do not clear the field first and then look. You look, and the field loses its grip.

wordByWord.meaning: weight, bulk — mass, not morality; named separately from the sin beside it
standing well around — used once in the New Testament and not found anywhere else
patience, endurance — one word, whichever of the two your translation prints
looking away to — present participle, an action that keeps going

relatedWords.meaning: to drag all around — the word for what was happening to Martha, and the exact reverse of looking away at one thing

modules.content: You do not clear the field and then look. You look, and the field loses its grip.

modules.heading: Martha, Martha
modules.content:
Luke's word for what happened to Martha is περισπάω (perispaō), and he uses it exactly once. It means to drag all around. Thayer's has it as being driven about mentally, distracted, over-occupied, too busy about a thing. The form in verse 40 is imperfect passive, which is to say it was being done to her, continuously — not a decision she made once and could unmake once.

That matters, because Martha is usually read as the cautionary figure in a story about priorities, and Jesus does not handle her that way. He says her name twice. Martha, Martha. The doubled name is a convention out of the Hebrew Scriptures — Abraham, Abraham, at the moment the knife is stopped; Moses, Moses, out of the bush — and the Gospels keep it. Simon, Simon, Jesus says, the night before Peter denies Him. It is how someone is addressed tenderly and urgently in the same breath. It is not the voice of a man scoring a point in an argument he has already won.

And the diagnosis is precise. Thou art careful and troubled about many things. Careful in the older sense the King James is using — full of care. Not you are doing the wrong work. Not serving is beneath your sister's calling. What gets named is the number. Many. One thing is needful.

Luke's placement is deliberate and almost nobody reads the two scenes together. This comes immediately after the Good Samaritan — a parable whose entire weight rests on the fact that the man who stopped to serve was the neighbour and the two who kept walking were not. Luke has just spent a paragraph commending the precise instinct Martha is acting on. He is not reversing himself a few verses later. The two stories hold each other up: serve, and know what the serving is for.

So the line being drawn is not between working and resting. It is between a life organised around many things and a life organised around one. Her hands were never the problem. Her hands were fine.

What Mary chose gets a peculiar description: that good part, which shall not be taken away from her. Set that against the anxiety running underneath the whole scene. Martha is worried about a meal that will be eaten and forgotten by tomorrow, served to a guest who is on His way to Jerusalem to die. Everything in the room is the kind of thing that gets taken away. Jesus names one that does not, and He names it to a woman who was too busy to sit down in front of it.

modules.videoTitle: SABBATH: Learn Why the Number 7 Is Used So Much in the Bible
modules.videoCaption: Five and a half minutes on why rest is where the creation account is heading rather than what it stops for — the seventh day is the one God blesses, and the pattern runs on through Scripture from there.

modules.heading: Where This Sits in the Story
modules.ancientTruth: This is the WILDERNESS stretch of God's story. Deuteronomy 8 looks back on forty years and gives the reason for them in one sentence: the LORD your God led you all the way in the wilderness, so that He might humble you and test you in order to know what was in your heart. The wilderness was not a detour from the promise. It was the schoolroom on the road to it.
modules.modernApplication: A season that takes away capacity — health, energy, the ability to do the work you are known for — reads as punishment from inside it. Hebrews takes up hardship directly a few verses after the anchor and is careful with the word it uses: what is described there is a father training sons, for their good, and not a judge sentencing enemies. Painful at the time, the passage says, and afterward a harvest.
modules.connectionPoint: Hosea puts it in the least likely register available: Therefore, behold, I will allure her and lead her to the wilderness, and speak to her tenderly. Allure is a courtship word. In that sentence the wilderness is not a sentence handed down; it is where a conversation can finally happen because nothing else is talking.
modules.newTestamentEcho: Jesus kept going there on purpose — He frequently withdrew to the wilderness to pray, Luke reports, in the middle of the busiest stretch of the ministry. And when the disciples came back from their own work He told them: Come with Me privately to a solitary place, and let us rest for a while. Mark gives the reason in the next breath: they did not even have time to eat.

modules.inlineImageAlt: A figure lying asleep and wrapped in a cloak beneath a desert tree at night, while a winged figure stands nearby holding a lamp and a small loaf. A crescent moon hangs above.
modules.inlineImageCaption: 1 Kings 19, after Elijah asked God to take his life: no answer to the prayer and no argument with it — an angel, bread baked on coals, and permission to lie down again. (The desert broom he sheltered under is a low shrub; the artist has given it a fuller canopy than it has.)

modules.heading: Bread, and Then Sleep, and Then a Word
modules.content:
The most instructive scene in Scripture about a person who has run out is not about a weak man. It is about Elijah, and it happens immediately after the greatest public success of his life.

In 1 Kings 18 fire falls at Carmel in front of the entire nation. In 1 Kings 19 he is running for his life. He leaves his servant behind at Beersheba, goes a day's journey into the wilderness alone, sits down under a broom tree, and asks to die. I have had enough, LORD. Take my life, for I am no better than my fathers.

What happens next is the part that gets skipped in every retelling.

God does not answer the prayer. God also does not correct the theology in it, and there is bad theology in it. There is no reminder of what had just happened on the mountain, no argument that the fear is disproportionate, no instruction to get up and be encouraged. What the text records is this: Then he lay down under the broom tree and fell asleep.

Then an angel touches him and says one thing. Get up and eat. There is a cake of bread baked over hot coals and a jar of water by his head. He eats. He drinks. He lies down again.

The angel comes back a second time with the same instruction, and this time a reason is attached. Get up and eat, or the journey will be too much for you.

Two meals, two sleeps, and no conversation at all. Only after that does he walk to Horeb, and only at Horeb does God finally speak — and even then not in the wind that shattered the rocks, not in the earthquake, not in the fire. After all of it, a still, small voice.

The order is the teaching. Food and sleep first. The word afterward. And when the word came it was quiet enough that a man still running would have walked straight past it.

There is a kind of person who reads that and feels accused rather than relieved, because it sounds like permission they have not earned. So it is worth being exact about what the passage does and does not claim. It does not say Elijah's collapse was admirable. It does not say the wilderness was a reward for good service. What it says is that God's first response to a man at the end of himself was bread, His second was more bread, and the reason given was the length of what was still ahead. The rest was not the end of the assignment. It was provisioning for it.

Deuteronomy 8 names what a wilderness is for, and people usually quote only the first half of the sentence. Forty years of being led, so that He might humble you and test you in order to know what was in your heart. The humbling is real and the passage does not soften it. But the sentence does not stop there and neither does the chapter: the hunger came so that the manna could come, and the manna came so they would learn that a person does not live on bread alone but on every word that comes from the mouth of the LORD.

Which is a strange way to teach that lesson — by feeding someone. And that is the shape of the thing. God does not usually remove a wilderness in order to teach in it. He teaches by what He supplies inside it, and what He supplies is nearly always smaller and more ordinary than what was asked for. Elijah asked to die and was given breakfast.

modules.heading: The Man Who Could Not Do His Work
modules.content:
John Milton's eyes had been failing for years before they failed completely. He said himself that they were naturally weak and that he was subject to frequent headaches, and that neither fact had ever slowed his reading down. By 1652 the sight was gone.

He had been warned. Asked to write a defence of the English people, he was told plainly by his physicians what it would cost him: he was already ill, already losing the remaining eye, and if he took the work on it would be irreparably lost. He wrote it anyway. Of the warning he later said only that "their premonitions caused no hesitation, and inspired no dismay."

So he got exactly the outcome he was told he would get. And what he wrote about it afterward, in his Second Defence of 1654, has an odd steadiness: "It is not so wretched to be blind, as it is not to be capable of enduring blindness." His own dark, he said, "keeps from my view only the coloured surfaces of things, while it leaves me at liberty to contemplate the beauty and stability of virtue and of truth."

That is the public version, written for an audience, in Latin, inside an argument he intended to win.

The private version runs to fourteen lines and it is not steady at all. Somewhere between 1652 and 1655 — the date has never been settled — he wrote a sonnet that opens with a man doing arithmetic on his own life and not liking the total. His light is spent before half his days. The one talent which is death to hide is lodged with him useless. His soul is more bent than ever to serve with it. And then the question, which he is honest enough to put into the poem rather than write around:

"Doth God exact day labour, light deny'd, I fondly ask."

Does God require the work and then take away the thing the work is done with. That is Martha's complaint in a different accent, and Milton knows it is a complaint — he calls his own asking foolish in the act of asking it.

The answer arrives before he has finished framing the question, and it does not address his eyes at all. "God doth not need either man's work or his own gifts."

Then the last line, the one everyone knows and almost nobody knows the setting of. Milton is not writing about contemplatives. He has just spent two lines on the thousands who speed at God's bidding and post over land and ocean without rest — the servants who can still work, and are working, and are not being criticised for it. And then, against them, not instead of them:

"They also serve who only stand and waite."

Also. The whole argument is in that one word. He is not claiming waiting is the better thing. He is claiming it counts.
modules.connectionToTheme: Milton's complaint and Martha's are the same complaint: I have been given something to do and I am being prevented from doing it. The answer he arrives at is the answer Jesus gives — that God is not short of labour, and what is being asked for was never output.

modules.heading: The Room
modules.content: Pascal put it in one sentence, in the fragments found after his death: "j'ai dit souvent que tout le malheur des hommes vient d'une seule chose, qui est de ne savoir pas demeurer en repos dans une chambre" — I have often said that all the unhappiness of men comes from one single thing, which is not knowing how to remain at rest in a room.
modules.historicalContext: Pensées, Lafuma 136 (Brunschvicg 139), from the sequence on divertissement — diversion. The version in general circulation, "all of humanity's problems stem from man's inability to sit quietly in a room alone," is a paraphrase rather than a translation: it adds the word alone, which the French does not contain, and hardens unhappiness into problems. Pascal's actual claim is narrower and worse. He is not saying people are bad at solitude. He is saying they cannot be at rest, and that they arrange their lives so as never to have to find out.

modules.heading: Pay Attention to What You Pay Attention To
modules.content:
There is a practice buried in all of this, and it is smaller than it sounds.

Pay attention to what you pay attention to.

Not pay attention to more things. Not feel guilty about the places your mind keeps returning to. Simply notice where it goes when nobody is steering it, and then ask why it goes there. Whatever your mind is on, it is on it for a reason, and the reason is usually available to anyone willing to look at it for thirty seconds instead of two.

That noticing is the first half. The second half is the part that gets skipped: take the reason to God instead of settling it privately. Not Lord, help me stop thinking about this, which is generally a request to be relieved of information. Something nearer to: this is where my mind goes; show me what it is doing there.

Because a mind is rarely wandering at random. It goes to what it is afraid of, what it is responsible for, what it has not finished, what it loves and cannot protect. A person lying awake at three in the morning is not being irrational. They are being informed, badly, by a system with no way to file the information and nobody to hand it to.

And this is where the words in this reading turn out to be one picture seen from three sides. εὐπερίστατος (euperistatos) is the thing standing all the way around a runner. περισπάω (perispaō) is a woman being dragged all around by many demands, in the passive, without having chosen it. ἀφοράω (aphoraō) is looking away from all of it at one thing. Each of the three is a statement about geometry — surrounded, encircled, pulled from every direction — and none of them is solved by fighting on every side at once. The answer given is to look at one thing until the circle stops being the place you live.

Which is not a technique for emptying the mind. Nothing in Scripture asks anyone for an empty mind. It is a question of what the mind is anchored to while it is full.

One caution, for anyone reading this in a season where the body will not cooperate. None of it is a promise that attention will fix the thing. Elijah's attention did not put fire back in his bones; he still had forty days of walking to do. Milton's did not restore his sight; he was still blind on the last line of the sonnet. What it changed, in both cases, was what the season turned out to be for.

modules.passage: And Jesus answered and said unto her, Martha, Martha, thou art careful and troubled about many things: But one thing is needful: and Mary hath chosen that good part, which shall not be taken away from her.
emphasis: which shall not be taken away from her
modules.scriptureContext: The correction and the promise arrive in the same breath, and the promise is about permanence — spoken to the one woman in the room who was busy with things that would not last the week.

modules.prompt: Where did your mind go this week when you were not directing it? Name the actual subject, not the feeling attached to it — and then ask the question that has probably never been asked out loud: why there?
additionalQuestions: What in your life right now is weight rather than sin — heavy, but not wrong? What would it cost to set it down for a season?
If someone said your name twice, gently, and told you that you were troubled about many things, would you agree with them?
Elijah was given food and sleep before he was given a word. What has God been providing that you have been treating as an interruption?

modules.heading: A Practice for Today
modules.instruction: A breath prayer, built from the two halves of Hebrews 12:1-2. Six slow breaths, no more. It is not a technique and it is not meant to produce a feeling — the words do the work, and the exercise is only holding still long enough to hear them.

steps.title: In
steps.description: Breathing in, silently: many things are standing all around me.

steps.title: Out
steps.description: Breathing out, silently: one thing is needful.

steps.title: Repeat
steps.description: Six times, slowly. If your mind goes somewhere on the third breath, do not drag it back. Note where it went. That is today's material, and it just told you something.

modules.inlineImageAlt: A narrow cleft between two dark rock walls, with pale light pouring through the opening from behind them.
modules.inlineImageCaption: A cleft in the rock with the light behind it. What Elijah heard at Horeb came after the wind, the earthquake and the fire had all finished, and it was quiet enough to walk straight past.

modules.heading: Looking at the Sun
modules.content:
Look at the sun — briefly, and not directly, and this is an illustration rather than an instruction — and then try to look at something else. You cannot, quite. The afterimage travels with your eyes. Whatever you turn toward, it is laid over the top of it. You have not stopped seeing other things. You are seeing them through the one thing.

That is nearer to what Hebrews 12:2 asks for than the word focus is. ἀφορῶντες (aphorōntes) is a present participle, a continuing look rather than a decision made once at the starting line. And it does not require that the rest of the world be cleared away first. Martha's house was still full of guests who needed feeding. Elijah still had a mountain to reach on foot. Milton never saw again. Nothing about anyone's circumstances was edited.

What changed was what everything else was seen through.

And the last thing worth noticing is who is being looked at. The sentence does not stop at Looking unto Jesus. It gives a reason: who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross. The same phrase turns up twice in two verses — the race is set before us, and the joy was set before Him. He ran it the way He is asking to be looked at. He endured by looking.

So this is not a discipline to be mastered by people with more grit than the rest of us. It is a Person to be looked at, and the same verse describes Him as having sat down. In a passage entirely about running, the one figure who is seated is the one everybody is watching.

Martha, for what it is worth, is not left where Luke leaves her. In John's Gospel she is on a road outside Bethany with her brother four days in the tomb, and she says the sentence that the whole scene in her kitchen had been making room for: I believe that You are the Christ, the Son of God, who was to come into the world. The correction in Luke was never a dismissal. It was the start of a conversation that took years, and she is the one who finishes it.

modules.heading: Closing Prayer
modules.prayerText: Lord, we have been careful and troubled about many things, and most of them were real. We are not asking You to make them stop mattering. We are asking to see them through You rather than in place of You. Where we are worn down, give us what You gave in the wilderness — bread, sleep, and a word afterward, in that order, which is not the order we would have chosen. Teach us to wait without calling it wasted. Give us patience, which is the same word as endurance in Your language even when it is not in ours. And hold our eyes, since we cannot hold them ourselves for very long. Amen.
modules.breathPrayer: Breathing in: many things stand all around me. Breathing out: one thing is needful.

modules.heading: Today's Commitment
modules.commitment: I will notice one place my mind keeps going this week, ask why it goes there, and bring the answer to God instead of managing it alone.
leavingAtCross: The belief that rest has to be earned before it is allowed
The weight that is heavy without being wrong, which I have been carrying because nobody told me to put it down
The suspicion that a season which took my strength was a punishment
receivingFromCross: Bread and sleep first, and a word after — in God's order, not mine
One thing that will not be taken away, in a week made of things that will
A seated Christ to look at while I am still running

modules.heading: One Question
modules.question: In Hebrews 12:1-2, what does the Greek word behind "Looking unto Jesus" actually describe?
options: A single decisive glance taken once, at the beginning
Looking away from everything else in order to fix the eyes on one thing, continuously
Studying Jesus' example carefully in order to copy His method
Closing the eyes to the world so that nothing else can be seen
modules.explanation: ἀφοράω (aphoraō) combines ἀπό (apo), away from, with ὁράω (horaō), to see — Thayer's glosses it as turning the eyes away from other things and fixing them on something. And the participle in Hebrews 12:2 is present tense, which in Greek carries continuing action. So it is neither a one-time decision nor a shutting out of the world; it is an ongoing look at one thing, which is what loosens everything else.

modules.heading: The Voice Behind Today
modules.name: Martha of Bethany
modules.era: first century, a village about two miles from Jerusalem
modules.bio: Sister of Mary and Lazarus, and by every indication the one who ran the household. She appears three times in the Gospels: welcoming Jesus into her home and being corrected there, meeting Him on the road after her brother's death, and serving at a supper in Bethany six days before the Passover — still serving, and not rebuked for it.
modules.keyQuote: Yes, Lord, I believe that You are the Christ, the Son of God, who was to come into the world.
modules.lessonForUs: Martha is the patron of everyone whose love takes the form of getting things done. What Jesus corrects in her kitchen is not the serving but the number of things she is being pulled between — and the woman He corrects is the woman He later draws one of the plainest confessions in the Gospels out of. Being told you are troubled about many things is not the same as being told you are the wrong kind of person.

modules.heading: Sources & Further Study

relatedScriptures.text: The full scene under the broom tree, including the second visit from the angel and the reason attached to it: "Get up and eat, or the journey will be too much for you."
The wilderness explained by the God who ran it — humbling and testing, and then manna, so that they would learn what a person actually lives on.
"I will allure her and lead her to the wilderness, and speak to her tenderly." The courtship verb, attached to the last place anyone would look for one.
"He maketh me to lie down in green pastures." The shepherd's first recorded action is making the sheep stop.
"In returning and rest shall ye be saved; in quietness and in confidence shall be your strength: and ye would not." The offer, and the refusal, in one verse.
"Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest." Rest offered as a Person rather than a schedule.
Where Martha ends up: on a road, four days too late by her own reckoning, saying the truest sentence in the chapter.

resources.title: John Milton, Sonnet 19 ("When I consider how my light is spent"), Poems, 1673
resources.description: Source of every line quoted in today's story, verbatim in Milton's original spelling as printed in the John Milton Reading Room text of the 1673 Poems. Composition is usually placed between 1652 and 1655 and has never been settled. The familiar title "On His Blindness" is not Milton's — it was supplied by an eighteenth-century editor.

resources.title: John Milton, Second Defence of the English People, 1654
resources.description: Source of the physicians' warning and the two lines on blindness. Written in Latin as Defensio Secunda pro Populo Anglicano; quoted here in Robert Fellowes's English translation, which is the standard one and is freely available online.

resources.title: Blaise Pascal, Pensées, Lafuma 136 / Brunschvicg 139
resources.description: The French is quoted verbatim from the divertissement sequence, with a plain English rendering beside it. The widely shared "sit quietly in a room alone" version is a paraphrase, not a translation — it adds a word Pascal did not write.

resources.title: Greek data
resources.description: aphoraō (G872) — "to look away from all else at one object"; two New Testament occurrences, Philippians 2:23 and Hebrews 12:2, where the form is a present participle. euperistatos (G2139) — a hapax legomenon; Thayer's glosses it "skilfully surrounding i.e. besetting, namely, to prevent or retard running" and notes it is not found elsewhere. ogkos (G3591) — "bulk, mass, hence a weight, burden." hypomonē (G5281) — "endurance, steadfastness, patient waiting for," rendered patience in the KJV and endurance in most modern versions. perispaō (G4049) — "to drag all around"; one New Testament occurrence, Luke 10:40, imperfect passive.

resources.title: Hebrew data
resources.description: qavah (H6960) — "to wait, look for, hope, expect," about forty-nine Old Testament occurrences. Brown-Driver-Briggs connects it to a root meaning to bind together, perhaps by twisting, and prints that derivation with "perhaps" attached; it is offered here with the same hedge the lexicon uses.

modules.forDeeperStudy: Read Hebrews 11 straight through before returning to 12:1-2, and watch what the cloud of witnesses actually consists of — chapter 11 says twice that they died without receiving what they were promised. Then read 1 Kings 18 and 19 in one sitting, without a break at the chapter division, and time how few verses separate the fire at Carmel from the request to die.
